verses.translation: And I trod{H1869} upon the sand{H2344} of the sea{H3220}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דָּרַכְתִּי (darakhti — 'I trod/marched', H1869) — the verb for treading a winepress (Isa 63:3), marching upon high places (Mic 1:3), and bending a bow (Jer 9:2). Greek TR has ἐστάθη ('he stood' — 3rd person, from ἵστημι). A back-translator from Greek 'stood' would write עָמַדְתִּי (amadti — 'I stood') from עמד, not the active martial verb דרך. The Hebrew implies purposeful treading, not static standing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 1st person 'I trod' (דרכתי). Greek TR: 3rd person ἐστάθη ('he/it stood') — the dragon is the subject. Some Greek manuscripts read ἐστάθην ('I stood' — 1st person), but even those use 'stood,' not 'trod.'
This verse is Greek 12:18. The Hebrew places it as 13:1, suggesting a different chapter-division tradition that ties the sand-of-the-sea vision to the sea-animal's emergence.
translation_notes: 'Trod' for darakh preserves the active, purposeful quality of the Hebrew verb — stepping/marching, not merely standing.
textual_notes: The Hebrew chapter division places the 'sand of the sea' as the opening of the sea-animal chapter, creating a narrative bridge: the visionary treads to the shore and watches the animal emerge. Greek attaches it to the end of chapter 12 as the dragon's action.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} animal{H2416} coming out{H3318} from the sea{H3220}, and it had seven{H7651} heads{H7218} and ten{H6235} horns{H7161}, and upon its horns{H7161} ten{H6235} crowns{H3804}, and upon its heads{H7218} names{H8034} of revilings{H2781} and blasphemies{H1442}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חַיָּה (chayyah — 'living creature/animal', H2416) — the generic OT word for wild animals (Gen 1:24-25, 7:14, 9:10). Greek θηρίον ('wild beast') carries inherent negativity. The Hebrew word is neutral — the same word describes the living creatures of creation. A back-translator from θηρίον would choose a negative term like חַיַּת רָעָה ('evil beast').

Uses TWO distinct blasphemy words: חֵירוּפִים (cherupim — 'reproaches/revilings', from חרף H2778) AND גִדּוּפִים (giddupim — 'blasphemies', from גדף H1442). Greek has only singular βλασφημίας ('blasphemy'). The Hebrew distinguishes between taunting reproach (cheruf — the Goliath-type taunt, 1 Sam 17:26) and outright blasphemy (gidduf). A back-translator from Greek's single word would use one Hebrew word, not two.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'names of revilings AND blasphemies' (two categories). Greek: 'names of blasphemy' (one category, singular βλασφημίας).
translation_notes: 'Animal' for chayyah rather than 'beast' — preserving the Hebrew word's neutrality. The word simply means 'living creature.'

חֵירוּפִים (cherupim) is a later Hebrew abstract-noun plural from חרף (H2778). The closest Strong's nominal form is H2781 (cherpah — 'reproach'). גִדּוּפִים (giddupim) is similarly a later plural from גדף (H1442).
textual_notes: Daniel 7:3-7 describes four animals (חֵיוָן in Aramaic, cognate of חַיָּה) rising from the sea with composite features. The Hebrew Revelation uses the same root vocabulary.

verses.translation: And the animal{H2416} that I saw{H7200} was like the likeness{H1823} of a horse{H5483}, and its feet{H7272} like the feet{H7272} of bears{H1677}, and its mouth{H6310} like the mouth{H6310} of the lion{H738}. And the dragon{H8577} gave{H5414} to it his power{H3581} and his throne{H3678} and great{H1419} might{H1369}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דְּמוּת (demut, H1823 — 'likeness/form'), the word from Genesis 1:26 ('Let us make man in our likeness') and Ezekiel's throne visions (Ezek 1:5, 1:16, 1:26, 8:2, 10:1). Greek ὅμοιον means simply 'similar to.' A back-translator would use דּוֹמֶה (domeh — 'resembling'), not the theologically loaded demut.

Uses תַּנִּין (tannin, H8577 — 'dragon/sea-serpent'), the OT chaos-monster (Gen 1:21, Ex 7:9-12, Isa 27:1, 51:9, Ezek 29:3, 32:2). Greek δράκων ('dragon') is a generic mythological term. The Hebrew tannin carries deep creation theology — it is the primordial sea-creature that YHWH created (Gen 1:21) and subdues (Isa 51:9, Ps 74:13).

Uses גְּבוּרָה (gevurah, H1369 — 'might/valor') where Greek has ἐξουσίαν μεγάλην ('great authority'). These are fundamentally different: Hebrew gevurah = raw power, martial strength, valor; Greek exousia = delegated authority, jurisdiction. A back-translator from Greek would use רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'authority'), not the warrior-word gevurah.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew has סוּס (sus — 'horse', H5483). Greek has παρδάλει ('leopard'). Daniel 7 has נָמֵר (namer — 'leopard'). The Hebrew substitutes 'horse' for 'leopard' — these are entirely different animals. The consonants ס-ו-ס bear no resemblance to נ-מ-ר; this cannot be a scribal or translation error. The Hebrew represents either a different textual tradition or a deliberate substitution, possibly connecting to the horse imagery elsewhere in Revelation (ch. 6, 9, 19).
Hebrew: 'great might' (גבורת גדולה). Greek: 'great authority' (ἐξουσίαν μεγάλην). Power vs. authority.
translation_notes: 'Likeness' for demut preserves the Genesis/Ezekiel creation-vision language.
'Dragon' for tannin — while tannin literally means 'sea-serpent/great reptile,' 'dragon' is used for consistency with its role as the supernatural adversary.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:4-6 lists lion, bear, and leopard as three of the four beasts. The Hebrew Revelation combines bear-feet and lion-mouth (matching Daniel) but substitutes horse for leopard. The horse may connect to the horse-riders of Revelation 6 and 9, or reflect a distinct Hebrew apocalyptic tradition.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} of its heads{H7218} resembling a wound{H2250} of death{H4194}, and the wound{H2250} was healed{H7495}; and all{H3605} the world{H5769} was astonished{H8074} on account of this animal{H2416}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חַבּוּרָה (chaburah — 'wound/stripe/bruise', H2250), the word from Isaiah 53:5: וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא לָנוּ ('and by his stripe we are healed'). Greek πληγή ('blow/plague') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use מַכָּה (makkah — 'blow/strike'), not the Isaiah 53 word. The Hebrew creates a dark parody: the animal's wound-healing mimics the Suffering Servant's healing.

Uses הָעוֹלָם (ha-olam — 'the world/age', H5769) where Greek has ὅλη ἡ γῆ ('the whole earth'). Hebrew olam has a temporal/eternal dimension ('age/eternity') absent from erets ('earth'). A back-translator from Greek would write כָּל הָאָרֶץ ('all the earth'), not ha-olam.

Uses מִשְׁתּוֹמֵם (mishtomem — 'was astonished/appalled', from שׁמם H8074). This verb also means 'to be devastated/desolated' — the same root as שְׁמָמָה (shemamah — 'desolation'). Greek ἐθαύμασεν ('marveled') is neutral or positive. The Hebrew carries horror and devastation; the Greek carries wonder and admiration.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'resembling a wound of death' (describes appearance). Greek: 'as though slain to death' (ὡς ἐσφαγμένην εἰς θάνατον — describes the act of slaughter). Different perspective.
Hebrew: 'was astonished on account of' (בשביל — causal). Greek: 'followed after' (ὀπίσω — directional). The Hebrew describes emotional response; the Greek describes physical following.
translation_notes: 'Wound' for chaburah preserves the Isaiah 53 echo. The same root appears in Isaiah 1:6 for Israel's unhealed wounds.
textual_notes: Isaiah 53:5 — 'he was wounded for our transgressions... and by his wound/stripe (chaburah) we are healed (nirpa).' The same chaburah+healing combination appears here applied to the animal — a counterfeit of the Servant's suffering.

verses.translation: And they prayed{H6419} to the dragon{H8577}, the one giving{H5414} the animal{H2416} power{H3581} and dominion{H4475}; and they prayed{H6419} to the animal{H2416} and said{H559}: Who{H4310} is like this animal{H2416}, and who{H4310} can{H3201} fight{H3898} with it?

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying', hitpael of פלל H6419). This is THE standard Hebrew verb for prayer to God (1 Sam 1:10, 1 Kings 8:28-30, Dan 6:10). Greek προσεκύνησαν means 'bowed down/worshipped' — a physical act. A back-translator from Greek would use הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ (hishtachavu — 'prostrated themselves'), not the prayer-specific hitpallel. The Hebrew makes the idolatry explicitly a form of PRAYER — people address the dragon and animal as one addresses God. This verb recurs throughout the chapter (vv. 5, 9, 13, 16) as a deliberate thematic marker.

'Who is like this animal?' (מי דומה לזאת החיה) echoes the most iconic Hebrew praise formula: מִי כָמוֹכָה בָּאֵלִם יְהוָה ('Who is like you among the gods, O YHWH?' — Ex 15:11). Also Psalm 35:10, 71:19, 89:6, 113:5. The Hebrew reader immediately recognizes this as a blasphemous parody of the Exodus victory song. Greek τίς ὅμοιος τῷ θηρίῳ carries no such literary echo.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'power and dominion' (כח וממשלה — two concepts). Greek: 'authority' (ἐξουσίαν — one concept). Hebrew has two words where Greek has one, and the Hebrew concepts (raw power + ruling dominion) differ from delegated 'authority.'
translation_notes: 'Prayed' for mitpallelim — this is not merely 'worshipped' but specifically prayer-worship, the verbal-spiritual act of directing prayer to a deity.
'Dominion' for memshalah (H4475) — from the root משל ('to rule'), used in Genesis 1:16 for the sun and moon's dominion over day and night.
textual_notes: The parody structure: In Exodus 15:11, Israel sings 'Who is like YHWH?' after the sea victory. Here, humanity asks 'Who is like the animal?' after the sea-animal emerges. The Hebrew inverts the Exodus narrative — from the sea comes not salvation but a counterfeit object of worship.

verses.translation: And it was given{H5414} to the animal{H2416} to open{H6605} its mouth{H6310} to speak{H1696} words{H1697} of wonders{H6381} and reproach{H2781}, until{H5704} the time of the forty{H705}-two{H8147} months{H2320} was finished{H3615}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נִפְלָאוֹת (nifla'ot — 'wonders/marvels', H6381) — the same word for God's miraculous deeds (Ex 3:20, 15:11, Ps 77:14, 78:12). Greek μεγάλα means merely 'great things.' A back-translator from Greek would use גְּדוֹלוֹת (gedolot — 'great things'), not the theologically loaded nifla'ot. The Hebrew implies the animal speaks words that counterfeit divine wonders.

Uses חֵירוּף (cheruf — 'reproach/reviling', from חרף H2778). This is the same noun family used for Goliath's taunting of Israel's armies (1 Sam 17:26) and Rabshakeh's taunting of YHWH (2 Kings 19:4). Greek βλασφημία is generic. The Hebrew specifies the TYPE of blasphemy: military-style taunting reproach.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'words of wonders and reproach' (miraculous claims + insults). Greek: 'great things and blasphemies' (μεγάλα καὶ βλασφημίας — generic greatness + blasphemy).

Hebrew: 'until the time was finished' (עד שכלא הזמן — temporal boundary). Greek: 'authority was given to it to act for forty-two months' (ἐξουσία ποιῆσαι μῆνας — mandate granted). Different framing: Hebrew gives a time limit; Greek gives a commission.
translation_notes: הַזְּמָן (ha-zeman — 'the time') is a post-biblical Hebrew word for 'appointed time,' common in Mishnaic Hebrew. No standard Strong's number. Its use here (rather than biblical עֵת or מוֹעֵד) reflects the text's late Second Temple linguistic stratum.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:25 — the little horn speaks 'great things' against the Most High for 'a time, times, and half a time' (= 42 months). The Hebrew Revelation follows Daniel's time frame while adding the specifically Hebrew nifla'ot vocabulary.

verses.translation: And he opened{H6605} his mouth{H6310} to revile{H2778} against YHWH{H3068} and against those dwelling in the heavens{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חָרֵף (charef, H2778 — 'to revile/taunt/reproach'), the verb for Goliath's defiance of Israel (1 Sam 17:10,25,26,36,45), Rabshakeh's taunting of YHWH (2 Kings 19:4,16,22; Isa 37:4,17,23), and Sennacherib's blasphemy (2 Kings 19:22 — 'Whom have you reviled and blasphemed?'). Greek βλασφημέω is generic. The Hebrew connects the animal's speech to Israel's most infamous blasphemers.

Uses the divine name יַהְוֶה (YHWH, H3068) where Greek has τὸν θεόν ('God'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֱלֹהִים (Elohim — 'God'), not the covenant name YHWH. The Hebrew text consistently uses the Tetragrammaton.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: two targets — YHWH and those dwelling in the heavens. Greek: three targets — God's name (τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ), his tabernacle (τὴν σκηνὴν αὐτοῦ), and those tabernacling in heaven. The Hebrew is more concise, omitting 'his name' and 'his tabernacle' as separate objects.
translation_notes: 'Revile' for charef — stronger than 'blaspheme,' carrying the specific sense of taunting, mocking, and verbally assaulting, as in a military challenge.

הַדָּרִים (ha-darim — 'those dwelling') uses a later Hebrew/Aramaic root for dwelling rather than the biblical יֹשְׁבִים (yoshvim, from ישב H3427). This form recurs throughout the Hebrew text (vv. 9, 13, 15).

verses.translation: And it was given{H5414} to it to fight{H3898} with the holy ones{H6918} and to overcome{H5329} them, and all{H3605} the peoples{H5971} and nations.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נִצֵּחַ (nitseyach, H5329 — 'to overcome/conquer'), the same root as מְנַצֵּחַ (menatseach) in the Psalm superscriptions ('for the choirmaster/conductor'). The root carries dual meaning: to lead/conduct AND to be victorious. Greek νικῆσαι ('to conquer') has only the victory sense. The Hebrew verb has a richer semantic range rooted in the Psalter.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all the peoples and nations' (עמים ואומים — 2 categories). Greek: 'every tribe and tongue and nation' (πᾶσαν φυλὴν καὶ γλῶσσαν καὶ ἔθνος — 3 categories). Greek adds 'tongue' (γλῶσσαν); Hebrew uses עמים ('peoples') rather than φυλή ('tribe').
translation_notes: 'Holy ones' for kedoshim — the standard OT term for those set apart for YHWH (Ps 34:9, Dan 7:18,21,25).
אוּמִים (ummim — 'nations') is a post-biblical Hebrew plural from אוּמָּה ('nation'), common in rabbinic literature. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:21 — 'this horn made war with the holy ones and prevailed against them.' The Hebrew Revelation follows Daniel's language directly.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} of them dwelling upon the earth{H776} pray{H6419} to it — those whose name{H8034} was not written{H3789} in the scroll{H5612} of life{H2416} of the lamb{H7716}, the slain one{H2026}, from the beginning of the creation{H1254} of the world{H5769}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בְּרִיאַת (beri'at — 'creation of', from ברא H1254) where Greek has καταβολῆς ('foundation/laying down'). Hebrew ברא is THE Genesis 1:1 verb — 'In the beginning God CREATED.' Greek 'foundation' implies construction; Hebrew 'creation' implies divine ex nihilo act. A back-translator from Greek would use יְסוֹד (yesod — 'foundation'), not ברא.

Uses הַנֶּהֱרָג (neherag — 'the slain one', from הרג H2026), the common verb for killing (Gen 4:8 — Cain killed Abel). Greek ἐσφαγμένου (from σφάζω) specifically means ritual slaughter. The Hebrew uses the general killing verb rather than a sacrifice-specific term like שָׁחַט (shachat — 'to slaughter ritually'). A back-translator from Greek σφάζω would choose שׁחט, not הרג.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'creation of the world' (בריאת העולם). Greek: 'foundation of the world' (καταβολῆς κόσμου). Different metaphors for the world's origin.
translation_notes: Again uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים ('pray') — maintaining the chapter's consistent prayer vocabulary where Greek has 'worship/bow down.'
'Scroll' for sefer (H5612) — scrolls were the standard writing format of the Hebrew period.
מִכִּתְחִילַּת (mikitchillat — 'from the beginning of') is a later Hebrew compound form. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Psalm 69:28 — 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living' (ספר חיים). Daniel 12:1 — 'everyone found written in the book.' The 'scroll of life' concept has deep OT roots.

verses.translation: Whoever{H4310} has ears{H241}, let him hear{H8085}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Whoever has ears hears' (מי שיש לו אזנים שומע — declarative present). Greek: 'If anyone has an ear, let him hear' (εἴ τις ἔχει οὖς ἀκουσάτω — conditional + imperative). The Hebrew states a fact; the Greek issues a command.
Hebrew: אָזְנַיִם (oznayim — 'ears', dual form for paired organs). Greek: singular οὖς ('ear').
translation_notes: The Hebrew literally says 'whoever has ears — he hears' (present tense, indicative). 'Let him hear' captures the exhortative force implied by context, though the Hebrew grammar is declarative.

verses.translation: If one{H259} leads into custody{H4929}, he shall go{H1980} into custody{H4929}; and if one{H259} kills{H2026} another{H312} soul{H5315} by the sword{H2719}, he shall be killed{H2026} by the sword{H2719}. And herein is the hope{H8615} and faithfulness{H530} of the holy ones{H6918}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תִּקְוָה (tiqvah — 'hope', H8615). Greek has ὑπομονή ('patience/endurance'). These are fundamentally different. Hebrew tiqvah is the great OT hope word (Jer 29:11 — 'plans to give you a tiqvah and a future'; 31:17 — 'there is tiqvah for your future'; Lam 3:29 — 'perhaps there is tiqvah'; Job 14:7 — 'there is tiqvah for a tree'). A back-translator from Greek ὑπομονή would use סַבְלָנוּת (savlanut — 'patience'), NOT the prophetic hope word. The Hebrew says retributive justice gives HOPE; the Greek says it requires PATIENCE. Entirely different theological orientations.

Uses מִשְׁמָר (mishmar — 'custody/guard-post', H4929) where Greek has αἰχμαλωσίαν ('captivity'). Hebrew mishmar is judicial/legal confinement (Gen 40:3-4 — Joseph in mishmar; 42:17 — brothers in mishmar; Lev 24:12; Num 15:34). Greek 'captivity' implies war-capture; Hebrew 'custody' implies legal detention. A back-translator from Greek would use שְׁבִי (shevi — 'captivity'), not the judicial term mishmar.

Adds נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh — 'soul/life', H5315): 'kills another soul by the sword.' Greek has no equivalent — simply 'kills by sword.' The Hebrew makes it explicitly about taking a person's life-breath, echoing Torah murder language: 'whoever strikes a nefesh' (Num 35:11,15,30).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'hope' (תקוה). Greek: 'patience' (ὑπομονή). Completely different concepts.
Hebrew: 'custody' (משמר). Greek: 'captivity' (αἰχμαλωσία). Different type of confinement.
Hebrew adds 'another soul' (נפש אחר) to the sword clause — absent in Greek.
translation_notes: 'Hope' for tiqvah is critical — the word Rachel named her son's city for (1 Chr 4:12), the word Jeremiah used to sustain exiles, the word Job clung to in suffering. It reframes the entire verse from endurance to expectation.
'Faithfulness' for emunah (H530) — from Habakkuk 2:4 ('the righteous shall live by his emunah'). Not merely 'faith/belief' but active fidelity and trustworthiness.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 15:2 — 'Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; those destined for captivity, to captivity.' The Hebrew Revelation echoes this retributive justice pattern.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} another{H312} animal{H2416} coming up{H3318} from the ground{H127}, and it had two{H8147} horns{H7161} like the lamb{H7716}, and it spoke{H1696} like the dragon{H8577}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah — 'ground/soil', H127) where Greek has γῆ ('earth/land'). As in Revelation 21:1, the Hebrew distinguishes between adamah (the soil from which Adam was formed, Gen 2:7; the soil cursed for Adam's sake, Gen 3:17) and erets (earth/land). The first animal rises from the sea (יָם); the second rises from the adamah. Greek uses γῆ for both concepts. A back-translator from Greek γῆ would use אֶרֶץ (erets), not the Genesis creation-word adamah. The adamah connects the second animal to the dust of human origin — it is an earth-born, human-derived creature, a counterfeit 'adam' rising from the 'adamah.'
translation_notes: 'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') preserves the Genesis creation distinction. The adamah/erets contrast carries the same theological weight as in Rev 21:1.
'Like the lamb' (כמו להשה) — the same word שֶׂה (seh H7716), the Passover lamb from Exodus 12:3-5, is used here. The second animal mimics the Lamb with counterfeit horns — a false Passover lamb.
textual_notes: The two animals form a counterfeit trinity: the dragon (counterfeit God), the sea-animal (counterfeit messianic ruler), and the ground-animal (counterfeit prophet who performs signs). The ground-animal's emergence from adamah — man's source material — makes it the most human of the three.

verses.translation: And it did{H6213} great{H1419} wonders{H6381} before{H6440} the first{H7223} animal{H2416}, and caused the ground{H127} and those dwelling upon it to pray{H6419} to the first{H7223} animal{H2416} whose wounds{H2250} were healed{H7495}.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses נִפְלָאוֹת (nifla'ot — 'wonders', H6381) — the divine miracle vocabulary. Combined with אותות ומופתים in v15, this creates the full Deuteronomy 13 false-prophet pattern: a prophet performs wonders and signs to entice to idolatry.

The personification of הָאֲדָמָה (adamah — 'the ground') as praying is striking. The Hebrew says the ground ITSELF and its inhabitants pray. In Greek, only the inhabitants worship (τοὺς ἐν αὐτῇ κατοικοῦντας). The Hebrew echoes the OT theme of creation's participation in both sin and redemption.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence' (τὴν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ πρώτου θηρίου πᾶσαν ποιεῖ) — this clause is absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew goes directly to the wonders.
Hebrew: 'whose wounds were healed' (חבורותיה — PLURAL 'wounds'). Greek: 'whose plague of death was healed' (ἡ πληγὴ τοῦ θανάτου — SINGULAR 'plague of death'). Different number and terminology.
translation_notes: The raw manuscript has a lacuna [    ] (empty brackets) before חבורותיה — a gap in the text, likely a missing preposition (מן — 'from'). This scribal gap is evidence of authentic manuscript transmission, not a polished back-translation.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 13:1-3 — 'If a prophet arises among you and gives you a sign or wonder (אות או מופת), and the sign or wonder comes to pass, and he says, Let us go after other gods... you shall not listen.' The ground-animal fulfills this false-prophet pattern exactly.

verses.translation: And it caused fire{H784} to fall{H5307} from the heavens{H8064} before{H6440} the man{H120}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses singular הָאָדָם (ha-adam — 'the man/mankind', H120 with the definite article), echoing Genesis where God walks with 'the adam.' Greek has plural τῶν ἀνθρώπων ('men'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲנָשִׁים (anashim — 'men') or בְּנֵי אָדָם (benei adam — 'sons of man'), not the Genesis-laden ha-adam. Same pattern as Rev 21:3.
greek_deviations: Hebrew omits 'great signs' (σημεῖα μεγάλα) and 'down to the earth' (εἰς τὴν γῆν) present in Greek. The Hebrew is notably more concise: fire falls from heavens before the man.
translation_notes: The fire from heaven echoes 1 Kings 18:38 (YHWH sends fire on Elijah's altar) and 2 Kings 1:10-12 (Elijah calls fire from heaven). The ground-animal counterfeits Elijah's prophetic power.

verses.translation: And it incited{H5496} the sons{H1121} of man{H120} with its signs{H226} and wonders{H4159}, and said{H559} to those dwelling upon the earth{H776} that they should make{H6213} a carved-image{H6459} for the animal{H2416} that has wounds{H2250} of the sword{H2719} and was healed{H7495}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses פֶּסֶל (pesel — 'carved-image', H6459) — the EXACT word from the Second Commandment: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶּסֶל ('you shall not make for yourself a carved-image', Ex 20:4, Deut 5:8). Greek εἰκόνα ('image') is neutral. A back-translator from Greek would use צֶלֶם (tselem — 'image') or דְּמוּת (demut — 'likeness'), not the Decalogue's specific prohibition word. The Hebrew author deliberately uses pesel, making the act an explicit violation of the Second Commandment.

CRITICAL: Uses הִסִּית (hissit — 'incited/enticed', hiphil of סות H5496) — the specific verb from Deuteronomy 13:6: 'If your brother... entices you (יְסִיתְךָ) secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods.' This is the Torah's technical legal term for enticement to idolatry. Greek πλανᾷ ('deceives/leads astray') is different — deception vs. active incitement. A back-translator from Greek would use הִתְעָה (hit'ah — 'led astray'), not the Deuteronomy 13 legal term.

CRITICAL: Uses the phrase אוֹתוֹת וּמוֹפְתִים (otot u-moftim — 'signs and wonders', H226+H4159) — the EXACT pair from Deuteronomy 13:1-2 where a false prophet gives 'a sign or a wonder' (אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵת) to entice to idolatry, and from the Exodus plagues (Deut 4:34, 6:22, 7:19, 26:8). Greek has only σημεῖα ('signs') — no 'wonders.' The Hebrew preserves the full Deuteronomy false-prophet formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'incited' (הסית). Greek: 'deceives' (πλανᾷ). Different verbs with different legal implications.
Hebrew: 'signs and wonders' (אותות ומופתים — full paired formula). Greek: only 'signs' (σημεῖα). Hebrew preserves the complete OT formula.
Hebrew: 'wounds of the sword' (חבורות חרב — plural). Greek: 'wound of the sword' (τὴν πληγὴν τῆς μαχαίρας — singular).
Hebrew: 'and was healed' (נתרפאה). Greek: 'and lived' (ἔζησεν — 'came back to life'). Healing vs. resurrection — different concepts.
translation_notes: 'Carved-image' for pesel captures the specific meaning: an idol carved from wood or stone, as prohibited in the Decalogue. Not merely an 'image' or 'representation.'
'Incited' for hissit carries the legal force of Deuteronomy 13 — criminal enticement to apostasy, punishable by death under Torah law.
textual_notes: The convergence of THREE Deuteronomy 13 elements — הסית (enticed), אותות ומופתים (signs and wonders), and פסל (carved-image) — shows the Hebrew author constructing the ground-animal as the ultimate Deuteronomy 13 false prophet. This cannot be reconstructed from the Greek text, which uses different vocabulary for all three.

verses.translation: And it was given{H5414} to it to give{H5414} to the carved-image{H6459} of the animal{H2416} spirit{H7307} and life-breath{H5315}, so that it could speak{H1696}, and to cause whoever was not willing{H7521} to pray{H6419} to the carved-image{H6459} of the animal{H2416} to be killed{H2026}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has BOTH רוּחַ (ruach — 'spirit/breath', H7307) AND נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh — 'life-breath/soul', H5315). Greek has only πνεῦμα ('spirit/breath'). This is the Hebrew two-part anthropology from Genesis 2:7 where God breathes into Adam and he becomes a נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה ('living soul'). The carved-image receives both spirit and soul — a grotesque parody of the Genesis creation of man. A back-translator from Greek πνεῦμα would use only רוּחַ, not add נֶפֶשׁ. The distinction between ruach and nefesh is a fundamentally Hebrew concept.

Uses יִרְצֶה (yirtseh — 'would be willing/desire', from רצה H7521), the verb for God's acceptance of sacrifices (Lev 1:3-4 — 'he shall offer it of his own will', לִרְצֹנוֹ). Greek has simply ἐὰν μή ('whoever does not'). The Hebrew adds the element of WILLINGNESS — the test is not whether one worships but whether one is WILLING to pray. רצה carries the sense of delight and willing acceptance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spirit and life-breath' (ruach ve-nefesh — two terms). Greek: 'spirit' (πνεῦμα — one term). The Hebrew has the fuller anthropological framework.
Hebrew: 'whoever was not willing to pray' (tests inner willingness). Greek: 'whoever does not worship' (tests outward action). Different standard: heart vs. act.
translation_notes: 'Spirit and life-breath' — ruach is the animating wind/breath from God; nefesh is the resulting life-being/soul. Together they constitute full animate existence.

The giving of ruach and nefesh to a pesel inverts Genesis 2:7 — God breathed into man; now a false prophet breathes into a carved idol. It also recalls Psalm 115:4-7 and 135:15-17 where idols have mouths but cannot speak. Here, the pesel is given what OT idols lack.

verses.translation: And it caused all{H3605} of them — the great{H1419} and the small{H6996}, the wealthy{H6223} and the poor{H6041}, the servants{H5650} and the freed — to receive one{H259} sign on his right{H3225} hand{H3027} or on their foreheads{H4696}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סִימָן (siman — 'sign/mark'), a later Hebrew word for a distinguishing mark or token. Greek χάραγμα (charagma — 'engraving/stamp') specifically means an engraved/branded mark (from χαράσσω — 'to engrave'). The Hebrew siman is a general sign or token; the Greek implies physical branding. Different types of marking.

CRITICAL: Uses עֲבָדִים וּמְשׁוּחְרָרִים ('servants and freed-ones'). Greek has ἐλευθέρους καὶ δούλους ('free and slaves'). Two major differences: (1) The ORDER is reversed — Hebrew puts servants first, then freed; Greek puts free first, then slaves. (2) The Hebrew term מְשׁוּחְרָרִים (meshuchrarim) is the specific legal term for manumitted slaves — those formally released from servitude (from the root שחרר). A back-translator from Greek ἐλεύθερος ('free man') would use בֶּן חוֹרִין (ben chorin — 'free-born'), not the legal manumission term. The Hebrew reflects Torah slave-law vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Pair order reversed throughout: Hebrew 'great and small, wealthy and poor, servants and freed.' Greek: 'small and great, rich and poor, free and slave.'
Hebrew: singular 'his right hand' (יד ימינו) but plural 'their foreheads' (מצחיהם). This grammatical number inconsistency is preserved from the source text.
translation_notes: 'Sign' for siman rather than 'mark' — preserving the Hebrew word's broader meaning as a distinguishing token.
'Freed' for meshuchrarim — not free-born people but formerly enslaved people who have been emancipated. A precise legal distinction.
textual_notes: The forehead-and-hand placement echoes Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18 — 'bind them as a sign (אות) on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.' The animal's sign parodies the Torah's tefillin commandment.

verses.translation: So that no one{H259} could buy{H7069} or sell{H4376}, except if he has this sign on his hand{H3027} or on his forehead{H4696}, or the name{H8034} of the animal{H2416}, or the number{H4557} of its name{H8034}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew repeats 'on his hand or on his forehead' from the previous verse. This repetition suggests the Hebrew verse division includes detail that Greek distributes across two verses.
translation_notes: קָנָה (qanah, H7069 — 'to buy/acquire') and מָכַר (makhar, H4376 — 'to sell') are standard OT commercial vocabulary (Gen 25:10, 47:20; Ruth 4:5; Prov 23:23).

verses.translation: Herein is wisdom{H2451} and understanding{H8394}: whoever is a master{H1167} of intelligence{H7922} must calculate{H2803} the number{H4557} of the animal{H2416}, for it is the number{H4557} of one{H259} man{H120}; and you shall find{H4672} the sum is six{H8337} hundred{H3967} and sixty{H8346} and six{H8337}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has THREE wisdom/intelligence words: חָכְמָה (chokhmah — 'wisdom', H2451) + תְּבוּנָה (tevunah — 'understanding', H8394) + שֶׂכֶל (sekhel — 'intelligence', H7922). Greek has only TWO: σοφία ('wisdom') + νοῦν ('mind'). The triple wisdom vocabulary is a distinctly Hebrew literary pattern: Proverbs 1:2 — 'to know wisdom and instruction, to discern words of understanding (tevunah)'; Daniel 1:17 — 'knowledge and intelligence (sekhel) in all literature and wisdom (chokhmah).' A back-translator from Greek's two terms would use two Hebrew terms, not three.

Uses בַּעַל שֶׂכֶל (ba'al sekhel — 'master of intelligence', H1167+H7922). The ba'al X idiom is a characteristically Hebrew construction: בַּעַל חֲלוֹמוֹת (ba'al chalomot — 'master of dreams', Gen 37:19). Greek ὁ ἔχων νοῦν ('the one having a mind') is flat by comparison.

Uses הַסַּךְ (ha-sakh — 'the sum/total'), a bookkeeping/accounting term for a calculated total. Greek has only ὁ ἀριθμός ('the number'). The Hebrew specifies the result is a computed sum — the product of gematria calculation.

Uses וְתִמָּצֵא (vetimmatse — 'and you shall find', niphal of מצא H4672). This is direct address to the reader: 'YOU will discover.' Greek states declaratively 'and his number IS...' The Hebrew makes it an interactive puzzle to be solved by the reader.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three wisdom terms (chokhmah + tevunah + sekhel). Greek: two (sophia + nous).
Hebrew: 'the number of one man' (אדם אחד — one specific individual). Greek: 'a number of a man' (ἀριθμὸς ἀνθρώπου — generic). The Hebrew specifies one particular person.
Hebrew: 'you shall find the sum' (interactive, addressed to reader). Greek: 'his number is' (declarative statement).
translation_notes: הַסַּךְ (ha-sakh) is a post-biblical accounting term (Mishnaic Hebrew) for 'the total/sum.' No standard Strong's number.
צָרִיךְ (tsarikh — 'must/needs to') is also post-biblical, common in Mishnaic Hebrew. These forms reinforce the text's late Second Temple linguistic stratum.
textual_notes: The number 666 in Hebrew gematria could correspond to various names. The Hebrew text's emphasis on 'one man' (adam echad) and its interactive 'you shall find' suggests the original audience knew which person was meant. Hebrew gematria and Greek isopsephia yield different name-candidates from the same number.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 13 in Hebrew is saturated with Torah legal vocabulary and OT prophetic echoes that cannot derive from the Greek text. The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers: (1) פֶּסֶל (pesel — 'carved-image') — the Second Commandment word, used three times for the idol (vv. 15-16), where Greek has neutral εἰκών; (2) הִסִּית + אוֹתוֹת וּמוֹפְתִים — the full Deuteronomy 13 false-prophet formula (enticement + signs and wonders) assembled in v15; (3) מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying') used four times for idol-worship (vv. 5, 9, 13, 16) where Greek has προσκυνέω ('bow down'); (4) חַבּוּרָה (chaburah — Isaiah 53:5 'wound/stripe') for the animal's wound; (5) תִּקְוָה (tiqvah — 'hope') vs. Greek ὑπομονή ('patience') in v11; (6) אֲדָמָה (adamah — 'ground') vs. γῆ ('earth') for the second animal's origin in v12; (7) רוּחַ וְנֶפֶשׁ ('spirit AND soul') vs. Greek's single πνεῦμα in v16; (8) triple wisdom vocabulary in v19 (chokhmah + tevunah + sekhel) vs. Greek's two terms; (9) מְשׁוּחְרָרִים (meshuchrarim — legal manumission term) vs. generic 'free' in v17; (10) סוּס (sus — 'horse') vs. πάρδαλις ('leopard') in v3; (11) 'Who is like this animal?' parody of Exodus 15:11; (12) the textual lacuna in v13 showing authentic manuscript transmission. The Deuteronomy 13 pattern is the most compelling: the ground-animal is constructed as the Torah's false prophet who performs signs and wonders (אותות ומופתים), incites (מסית) the people, and commands them to make a carved-image (פסל) — the full legal framework of enticement to idolatry. No back-translator from Greek could independently reconstruct this coherent Torah-law pattern using precisely the Deuteronomy 13 vocabulary for all three elements.
